front: Phase of the resistor's voltage vs the series current?
back: In phase.

front: Phase of the inductor's voltage vs the series current?
back: Eₗ LEADS the current by 90°.

front: Phase of the capacitor's voltage vs the series current?
back: Ec LAGS the current by 90°.

front: What is the phase relationship between Eₗ and Ec in series?
back: 180° apart — exactly opposite, so they subtract.

front: What is the same through every part of an RLC series circuit?
back: The current.

front: How do Xl and Xc combine in series?
back: They subtract: net X = Xl − Xc. The smaller is eliminated, the larger reduced.

front: Impedance formula for RLC series?
back: Z = √(R² + (Xl − Xc)²)

front: R 12 Ω, Xl 24 Ω, Xc 8 Ω. Z?
Xc is larger than Xl. Does the negative difference matter in Z?
back: No — it's squared. R 10, Xl 30, Xc 54 → √(100 + 576) = 26 Ω.

front: Two common Z mistakes in RLC series?
back: Adding Xl + Xc, or putting Xl and Xc separately into √(R² + …). Always subtract first.

front: Why can RLC series current be surprisingly large?
back: Xl and Xc cancel, so Z can be smaller than either reactance.

front: RLC example on 240 V: current and drops?
Can a component's voltage exceed the supply in RLC series?
back: Yes — Eₗ = 288 V on a 240 V supply. Eₗ and Ec partly cancel, so the supply only provides the difference.

front: Total voltage formula in RLC series?
back: Eₜ = √(Eᵣ² + (Eₗ − Ec)²)

front: L and C values in Example 23–1?
66.3 µF, 0.0663 H, 8 Ω on 120 V, 60 Hz. Current?
Xl 62 Ω, Xc 38 Ω on 208 V. What R limits current to 8 A?
Power quantities in Example 23–1?
back: P 1728 W; VARsL 3456; VARsC 1152; net 2304 VARs inductive; VA 2880.

front: Apparent power formula in RLC circuits?
back: VA = √(P² + (VARsL − VARsC)²)

front: Why do inductive and capacitive VARs cancel?
back: While the coil stores energy the capacitor releases it (and vice versa) — they trade energy locally, so the source supplies only the net.

front: Book typo in Figure 23–6?
back: VARsC shown as 1142; correct value is 1152 (96 V × 12 A). Also "PF = 0.06 × 100" should be 0.6.

front: When is the RLC series PF lagging?
back: When inductive VARs (Xl) exceed capacitive VARs (Xc) — current lags.

front: When is the RLC series PF leading?
back: When capacitive VARs (Xc) exceed inductive — current leads.

front: Example 23–1 PF and θ?
18 W, 24 VARsL, 34 VARsC in series. PF, leading or lagging?
back: Net 10 VARs capacitive → PF = 18/√(18² + 10²) ≈ 87.4% LEADING.

front: tan θ in an RLC series circuit?
back: tan θ = (Xl − Xc)/R = (VARsL − VARsC)/P

front: What is resonance?
back: The frequency at which Xl = Xc, so they cancel completely.

front: Why must Xl and Xc be equal at some frequency?
back: Xl rises with frequency and Xc falls — the curves must cross.

front: Resonant frequency formula?
back: fR = 1 / (2π√(LC))  (L in H, C in F)

front: Formulas for the L or C needed to resonate at fR?
back: L = 1/(4π²f²C); C = 1/(4π²f²L) — both π and f squared.

front: C needed to resonate with 0.2 H at 1200 Hz?
L needed to resonate with 50 µF at 400 Hz?
At series resonance, what are Z, current and PF?
back: Z = R (minimum), current maximum, PF = 100% (θ = 0°).

front: 0.0159 H (5 Ω wire) + 1.59 µF on 50 V: current at resonance (1000 Hz)?
back: Only R limits it: 50/5 = 10 A (vs ~0.47 A at 600 Hz, ~0.73 A at 1400 Hz).

front: In that circuit, the voltage across L and across C at resonance?
back: 10 A × 100 Ω = 1000 V each — on a 50 V supply.

front: At resonance, do L and C disappear?
back: No — they cancel each other's effect on the source, but each carries full current and develops a full (high) voltage.

front: What is bandwidth?
back: The frequency range between the two points where current is 0.707 × maximum: B = f₂ − f₁.

front: Bandwidth formula using Q?
back: B = fR / Q

front: High-Q vs low-Q resonant circuit?
back: High Q (low R): sharp peak, narrow bandwidth. Low Q: flat peak, wide bandwidth.
extra_notes: Bandwidth is inversely proportional to Q

front: Resonance at 1000 Hz, 0.707 points at 995 and 1005 Hz. Bandwidth?
back: 10 Hz (narrow — high Q)

front: Resonance at 1200 Hz, 0.707 points at 1150 and 1250 Hz. Bandwidth?
back: 100 Hz (wide — low Q)

front: Why can PF capacitor banks cause trouble on systems with VFDs?
back: Capacitors + system inductance form a resonant L-C circuit; if it lands near a harmonic (300, 420 Hz…) currents/voltages are magnified — blown fuses, failed caps. Hence detuned banks.

front: How do resonant AC test sets produce very high test voltages?
back: A tuned reactor resonates with the cable's capacitance; at resonance the voltage across the cable is magnified (≈ Q × supply).

front: What is ferroresonance?
back: Resonance between an iron-core transformer's (nonlinear) inductance and cable capacitance — often after single-phase switching — producing erratic overvoltages.

front: 400 Hz resonant HV source: 15 mH, 2 Ω, 240 V. Capacitor voltage rating?
back: At resonance I = 240/2 = 120 A; Ec = I × Xc (= I × Xl ≈ 120 × 37.7 Ω). The rating must exceed THAT (×1.414 if DC-rated), not 240 V.

front: Review Q4 (400 Hz): what must you NOT use?
back: 377 — compute 2π × 400 for Xl and Xc.
